title: T1 — Core Terraform workflow
bodyMarkdown:
## Core Terraform workflow

Exam group **3**. Group 2 covered what providers and state are; this group is the command-line loop you actually run against them: initialize, validate, plan, apply, destroy, and keep the files formatted. Every command here is safe to run without credentials except `apply` and `destroy`, which this workbook never runs against real cloud accounts.

### tf.004.3a — Describe the Terraform workflow

HashiCorp describes Terraform's core workflow in three stages. Write: "Author infrastructure as code." Plan: "Preview changes before applying." Apply: "Provision reproducible infrastructure." You write configuration in an editor, Terraform previews exactly what it intends to do before touching anything, and only the apply stage actually provisions or changes real infrastructure — nothing in the write or plan stage can change a live resource.

On a team, each stage gets a collaboration step layered on top. At write time, members "save their changes to version control branches to avoid colliding with each other's work," the same branch-per-change habit used for any shared codebase. At plan time, "Terraform's plan output creates an opportunity for team members to review each other's work" as part of the pull request, so a reviewer sees the concrete add/change/destroy actions before merging, not just the configuration diff. At apply time, it matters that a merged pull request's plan can be stale, because the shared branch or the state file may have moved since the review; the practice is to "review the final concrete plan that's run against the shared team branch and the latest version of the state file" immediately before applying, rather than trusting the plan that was reviewed earlier in the pull request.

The discriminator: write, plan, and apply are not three names for the same action performed three times — write only produces configuration, plan only produces a proposal that reads current state but changes nothing, and apply is the one stage that is allowed to create, modify, or destroy a real object.

**Exam tip:** if a stem describes editing `.tf` files, that is the write stage; "preview what would change without changing anything" is the plan stage; "a pull request's plan can be out of date by the time it is merged" is testing the team-workflow addition to apply, not a new command.

### tf.004.3b — Initialize a Terraform working directory

"The `terraform init` command initializes a working directory containing Terraform configuration files," and it is "the first command you should run after writing a new Terraform configuration" or after cloning one from version control. Running it again later is not destructive: "It is safe to run this command multiple times."

Init does two independent jobs in the same run. First, backend initialization: "the root configuration directory is consulted for backend configuration and the chosen backend is initialized" (remote backends are a later objective; the default backend is the local state file from group 2). Second, dependency installation: Terraform "searches the configuration for module blocks, and retrieves the source code for referenced modules," and separately "searches...for both direct and indirect references to providers and attempts to install the plugins for those providers" (module and provider syntax themselves are groups 5 and 2). Once a provider is installed, "After successful installation, Terraform writes information about the selected providers to the dependency lock file."

A plain re-run does not touch what is already there: re-running init "will install the sources for any modules that were added to configuration since the last init," "but will not change any already-installed modules." That is why init must be run again whenever a configuration adds a new module or provider requirement, changes its backend block, or otherwise needs new dependencies — a bare re-run only adds what is missing.

One flag deliberately breaks that stability. "Use `-upgrade` to override this behavior, updating all modules to the latest available source code," and for providers it makes Terraform "ignore any selections recorded in the dependency lock file," choosing instead to "take the newest available version matching the configured version constraints." Two teammates who run a plain `terraform init` on the same lock file get identical provider versions; a teammate who runs `terraform init -upgrade` can walk away with a newer version even though nothing in the configuration changed.

The discriminator: init installs and initializes dependencies but never checks whether the configuration is internally correct, and it never reads or changes real infrastructure the way `plan` and `apply` do — it only prepares the working directory so those later commands have something to work with.

**Exam tip:** "missing provider/module, or a new backend, before anything can run" is an `init` question; "a plain re-run picked up a newly added module but left an already-installed one alone" is `init` without `-upgrade`; "a machine ended up with a newer provider version even though the lock file was committed" is `-upgrade`.

### tf.004.3c — Validate a Terraform configuration

`terraform validate` checks a configuration against itself, not against the outside world. It runs checks that "verify whether a configuration is syntactically valid and internally consistent, regardless of any provided variables or existing state," which is "primarily useful for general verification of reusable modules, including correctness of attribute names and value types." Critically, it "does not validate remote services, such as remote state or provider APIs" — validate cannot tell you whether a resource type still exists on the provider's side, whether your credentials work, or what would actually change.

Because it checks attribute names and types against a provider's schema, validate still needs "an initialized working directory with any referenced plugins and modules installed" before it can run; it needs the plugin present to know that schema, even though it never calls out to that plugin's remote API. That is why a directory initialized only far enough for validation (`terraform init -backend=false`, skipping backend setup) is enough — validate needs the provider plugin, not a working backend or live credentials.

The discriminator: `validate` catches syntax errors and wrong attribute names/types without ever touching a real account; `plan` (3d) goes further and reads live remote state, which means plan needs credentials and can fail for reasons validate would never catch, and validate can pass on a configuration that later fails to plan or apply because of something only the real platform knows.

**Exam tip:** "catches a typo'd attribute name or malformed block with no credentials and no network call" is `validate`; "needs to reach the actual cloud account to know what to do" is `plan`, not `validate`.

### tf.004.3d — Generate and review an execution plan

`terraform plan` "creates an execution plan, which lets you preview the changes that Terraform plans to make." Building that preview takes two steps: it first "Reads the current state of any already-existing remote objects to make sure that the Terraform state is up-to-date," then compares that refreshed state against the configuration and "Proposes a set of change actions that should, if applied, make the remote objects match the configuration." Those proposed actions are reported as add, change, or destroy; when an attribute cannot be changed in place, Terraform proposes destroying the existing object and creating a new one in its place, shown as a single "replace" action rather than as separate destroy and add lines.

Plan is only a preview: "The plan command alone does not actually carry out the proposed changes." Nothing about running `plan`, by itself, ever creates, modifies, or destroys a real object.

A plan can be saved to a file with `-out`, which "Writes the generated plan to the given filename in an opaque file format," one "you can later pass to `terraform apply`" (3e) to run exactly what was reviewed. `-target` narrows the preview: it "Instructs Terraform to focus its planning efforts only on resource instances which match the given address" and whatever they depend on, rather than the whole configuration. `-refresh-only` mode never proposes changing real infrastructure at all; it only exists to "update the Terraform state and any root module output values to match changes made to remote objects outside of Terraform," i.e. to reconcile Terraform's own record after something changed the resource by hand. `-destroy` mode previews the opposite of a normal plan: it "Creates a plan whose goal is to destroy all remote objects that currently exist, leaving an empty Terraform state," without destroying anything yet.

Version note: `-destroy` has always worked on `plan`, but `apply` gained it later. HashiCorp's destroy-command page states the boundary precisely: "The `-destroy` option to `terraform apply` exists only in Terraform v0.15.2 and later." (The `plan` command's own page states the same cutover more loosely, as holding "in Terraform v0.15 and earlier" — use the destroy page's 0.15.2 if a question asks for the exact version.) Before Terraform 0.15.2, the only way to actually execute a destroy plan was `terraform destroy` itself (3f). Current Terraform accepts `-destroy` on both `plan` and `apply`.

The discriminator: `plan` only reports what would happen — add, change, destroy, or replace — and a saved `-out` file is what turns that report into something `apply` can execute later without recomputing it.

**Exam tip:** "add, change, destroy, or a resource shown being destroyed and re-created together" (replace) is what `plan` reports; "only check part of the configuration" is `-target`; "only reconcile state after a manual change, without touching real infrastructure" is `-refresh-only`; "preview a full teardown before running it" is `plan -destroy`.

### tf.004.3e — Apply changes to infrastructure with Terraform

"The `terraform apply` command executes the operations proposed in a Terraform plan." Run without a saved plan file, apply "automatically creates a new execution plan as if you had run [`terraform plan`]," then "prompts you to approve that plan, and performs the indicated operations" only once you confirm.

"You can pass the `-auto-approve` option to instruct Terraform to apply the plan without asking for confirmation," which is what lets apply run unattended in a script or pipeline — but it means whatever the freshly generated plan proposes is carried out with no human check at that moment.

Applying a plan file previously saved with `plan -out` (3d) behaves differently again: Terraform does not regenerate the plan or prompt at all, it simply "performs the operations in the saved plan without prompting you for confirmation," running exactly what was already reviewed when the file was created, even if the real infrastructure has since drifted (changed outside Terraform since the plan was made). `-auto-approve` and a saved plan file both skip the interactive prompt, but for different reasons — one accepts a plan generated in that same run sight-unseen, the other executes a plan someone already reviewed earlier.

Apply also accepts `-destroy` directly: it "creates a plan to destroy all remote objects" as one of apply's own planning modes, then carries that plan out like any other apply.

The discriminator: an interactive `apply` always shows you a freshly computed plan and waits for "yes"; `-auto-approve` keeps the fresh computation but drops the wait; applying a saved `-out` file drops both the fresh computation and the wait, because approval already happened when the file was written.

**Exam tip:** "ran unattended in CI with no prompt, computing its own plan each time" is `-auto-approve`; "applied exactly the plan a teammate already reviewed, without recomputing it" is applying a saved `-out` file.

### tf.004.3f — Destroy Terraform-managed infrastructure

"The `terraform destroy` command deprovisions all objects managed by a Terraform configuration." It is not a separate engine from apply: "This command is just a convenience alias for the following command: `terraform apply -destroy`" on current Terraform versions (see the 3d version note for the pre-0.15.2 exception, when `apply` did not accept `-destroy` and `terraform destroy` was the only way to run one).

`terraform destroy` also accepts `-target` directly: "You can use the `-target` option to destroy a particular resource and its dependencies," for example `terraform destroy -target aws_instance.example`. That gives three distinct ways to end up with fewer managed objects, and this objective's discriminator is telling them apart. Plain `terraform destroy` builds and applies a plan against every object the configuration currently manages, ending in an empty state. `destroy -target` removes one named resource (and whatever depends on it) without touching the configuration file at all. Deleting that resource's block from the configuration and then running an ordinary `terraform apply` also removes just that one resource, but by editing the configuration first rather than by naming the resource on the command line: plan compares the edited configuration, which no longer describes that resource, against state, and proposes destroying only the object no longer described — every other managed resource is left alone either way.

**Exam tip:** "tear down everything a configuration manages" is `terraform destroy` (equivalently `apply -destroy`); "remove just one resource, by name, without editing any file" is `destroy -target`; "remove just one resource by editing the configuration first" is deleting its block and running a normal `apply`.

### tf.004.3g — Apply formatting and style adjustments to a configuration

"The `terraform fmt` command formats Terraform configuration file contents so that it matches the canonical format and style." "This command applies a subset of the Terraform language style conventions, along with other minor adjustments for readability." That is all it does: it only rewrites spacing, alignment, and quoting, and it has no way to detect a bad attribute name or type, because nothing on the fmt command's own doc page describes checking whether a configuration is correct or valid — that is `validate`'s job (3c), not fmt's. A file can be perfectly formatted and still fail `validate`, and a file can pass `validate` while still being badly formatted — the two commands check unrelated properties.

By default fmt is shallow: "By default, the command only processes the specified, or current, directory." Add `-recursive` and it also "processes files in subdirectories in addition to the current directory," which matters once a configuration is split across modules in nested folders.

`-check` changes what fmt does instead of rewriting files: it "checks if the input is formatted. The exit status is `0` if the command's input is properly formatted," and otherwise the exit status is non-zero and Terraform lists the improperly formatted file names — this is the flag a CI (continuous integration) pipeline uses to fail a build on bad style without fmt silently rewriting a contributor's files in the process.

The discriminator: `fmt` only ever touches whitespace and layout and never reports a configuration error; `validate` only ever reports syntax and schema errors and never rewrites a file. Passing one says nothing about the other.

**Exam tip:** "rewrote indentation and alignment across a directory tree" is `fmt -recursive`; "failed a CI job because a file wasn't canonically formatted, without changing the file" is `fmt -check`; "caught a bad attribute name" is `validate`, never `fmt`.

### Warnings

- Do not run `terraform apply` or `terraform destroy` against real cloud credentials in this workbook; `terraform fmt`, `terraform validate`, `terraform init -backend=false`, and `terraform plan` (without credentials configured) are the commands safe to run freely.
- Never call `ExecuteTerraformCommand` or `ExecuteTerragruntCommand` from this workbook's tools.
- `-auto-approve` and applying a saved plan file both skip the interactive prompt; treat either as a real apply, never as a dry run.
